pattern.crimePattern: shop manager diverting customer payments to his own number kills the owner who found out
pattern.notes: "The till isn't working, pay this number" is a widely reported everyday fraud. Fictional shop on a real street; fictional mobile-money service and network.

ob.reportedBy: Abubakar Hassan, shopkeeper, Biashara Street, Mombasa
ob.text: Abubakar Hassan, a shopkeeper on Biashara Street, reports that his neighbour Mwanajuma Athman (58), owner of Kanga za Pwani, was found dead in the back store of her shop at 13:35, during Friday prayers.

people.name: Mwanajuma Athman
people.bio: Widow. Thirty-one years selling kanga on Biashara Street. Does her own books every Friday while the street is at prayer.

facts.text: Abubakar Hassan found Mwanajuma Athman dead in the back store of Kanga za Pwani at 13:35, during Friday prayers.
Mwanajuma was struck with the shop's brass-tipped measuring rod.
Two glasses of spiced tea on the counter, one finished, one barely touched. She was expecting a visitor during prayers.
An empty envelope in her drawer: 'PesaPap Business — July statement'. The statement itself is gone.
Her will: the shop goes to her daughter and her nephew Faiz, jointly. Dancan isn't named.
Wage book: 'D. Odhiambo — paid in full to end of July.'
Stock book: one bale 'missing' in July. Clipped behind it, the supplier's note: 'Bale found at our Malindi depot, sending back.'
A cardboard sign under the counter: 'TILL HAIFANYI KAZI — LIPA NAMBA HII: 07xx xxx 418' (the till isn't working, pay this number).
Rent card for the flat upstairs: tenant R. Hamisi, June and July unpaid. In Mwanajuma's hand: 'Pay when you can.' Dancan doesn't live in the building.
Abubakar: he went to the mosque at 12:30. Mwanajuma stayed in, as every Friday, to do her books. At 13:35 her shutter was half down and the back light on. He went in and found her.
Abubakar: on Tuesday her nephew Faiz shouted at her in the street about his late uncle's share of the shop.
Pili's phone: 'Confirmed. KSh 6,400 sent to DANCAN ODHIAMBO 07xx xxx 418.' Twice this month Dancan told her the till was broken and to pay his number.
Pili's phone also shows her paying stallholders at Marikiti market at 12:40 and 13:05.
PesaPap, 07xx xxx 418: 112 incoming customer payments since December, KSh 341,900, mostly on Saturdays, each withdrawn at agents the same evening.
Jamii Mobile, 07xx xxx 418, Friday: on the Biashara mast 12:30–13:20, then Mwembe Tayari from 13:28.
Kassim: Dancan arrived at the Mwembe Tayari bus park at 13:30, sweating, and said three times that he had "been waiting here an hour".
Ustadh Salim: Faiz recited before the sermon and stayed through prayers and the committee tea, about 12:20 to 13:40, in front of several hundred people.
Ustadh Salim: the shopkeepers of Biashara Street, Abubakar Hassan among them, prayed in the front rows from about 12:35.
Maternity home register: R. Hamisi signed in at 11:40 as birth companion for her sister, out at 15:20. The nurse says she never left.
Dancan: "I was at Mwembe Tayari from half past twelve, waiting for the Malindi bus with our stock."
Dancan: "The till works fine. Mama handled all the money."
Dancan admits he was at the shop at about one o'clock, "for a minute". He says she was fine when he left.
Dancan: "Sometimes the till was slow. I was helping customers."
Faiz: "I was in the mosque."
Faiz: the will gives him half. "I wanted to run it now, not when she's dead. I'm ashamed of what I said on Tuesday."
Rukia: "I was with my sister. She had a baby girl at two o'clock."

interrogations.intro: Dancan arrives from Mwembe Tayari with two bales on a handcart and stops at the tape. "Mama? Mama Mwanajuma?"

topics.reply: Six years I worked for her. She trusted me with everything.
Statements? Mama did the books. I sold cloth.
Her nephew wants the shop. On Tuesday he shouted at her in the street. Everybody heard.
Ask Kassim, the supplier at the bus park. He saw me there. I was waiting an hour.

interrogations.intro: Faiz is still in his prayer clothes. He won't sit down. "I shouted at her on Tuesday. The last thing I did was shout."

topics.reply: Half the shop, one day. I wanted to run it now, not when she's dead. I'm ashamed of what I said.
Ask Ustadh Salim. I recited before the sermon. Three hundred people watched me.

interrogations.intro: Rukia takes the call in a maternity corridor, a newborn crying behind her. "I am with my sister. What is it?"

topics.reply: Mama Mwanajuma told me to pay when I can. She was like that. Who does that any more?

interrogations.intro: Abubakar sits on his own step with his hands in his lap. "Forty years next door. Every Friday she stayed in with her books."

topics.reply: The manager. Polite boy. On Saturdays he runs the shop alone and it is always full.

interrogations.intro: Pili answers from Marikiti market. "Dancan? Yes, I know him. The till never works when I come."

topics.reply: That sign! Twice this month he told me the till was broken and to pay his number. Look, here are the messages.

contradictions.reaction: I passed the shop at one. For a minute. To collect the bale list. She was fine when I left. She gave me tea.
Sometimes the till was slow. Customers were waiting. I was helping them. I was going to give her the money.

words.text: she found out he was diverting the shop's payments to his own number
she was cutting him out of the inheritance
she was about to evict him
she accused him of stealing a bale

prosecutor.pass: The mast puts him on Biashara Street during prayers, and he admits the shop. He did it.
fail: Doesn't hold up. A nephew who shouted on Tuesday was in front of three hundred people on Friday. Who was on that street?
No. Read his phone against his story. Where was it at one o'clock?

prosecutor.pass: Three hundred and forty thousand shillings, two glasses of tea. Clean.
fail: He did it. Now tell me why, or his lawyer will tell the court a story.
That motive isn't his. Whose statement is missing from that drawer, and what was in it?

proof.concludes: Mwanajuma was alone in the shop during prayers, 12:30 to 13:35, and she had made tea for a visitor.
Dancan said he was at Mwembe Tayari from 12:30, but his phone was on the Biashara mast until 13:20. Pressed, he admits being at the shop at one.
For eight months he had customers pay his own number: 112 payments, KSh 341,900. The July statement that would have shown it is gone. Dancan Odhiambo killed her because she had found out.

eliminations.why: Faiz was reciting and praying at the mosque from about 12:20 to 13:40, in front of several hundred people.
Rukia was at the maternity home from 11:40 to 15:20 and never left her sister.
Abubakar was praying in the front rows from 12:35.
Pili was paying stallholders at Marikiti market at 12:40 and 13:05.
The will concerns her daughter and Faiz. Dancan has no claim to be cut out of.
Dancan doesn't live there. The tenant is Rukia, and Mwanajuma had told her to pay when she could.
His wages were paid in full to the end of July.
The "missing" bale turned up at the supplier's Malindi depot.

reconstruction.text: December. On busy Saturdays a cardboard sign appears on the counter: "The till isn't working, pay this number." The number is Dancan's.
Thursday. Mwanajuma reads the shop till's July statement. On the days Dancan ran the shop, the takings collapse.
Friday, 12:30. The street goes to prayer. She makes two glasses of tea and waits for him.
About 12:55. She shows him the statement and says she will go to the police tomorrow. He picks up the measuring rod.
He takes the statement, leaves by the back alley and walks to Mwembe Tayari, where he tells a supplier three times that he has been waiting an hour.

tier1.line: A sign under the counter, a number on it. Ask a regular customer what she paid to.

tier2.line: He says Mwembe Tayari from half past twelve. A mast tells you the neighbourhood, not the door. Which neighbourhood was his phone in?

tier1.line: Something is missing from her drawer. What would a July statement show?

tier2.line: A hundred and twelve payments to his number, and the statement that would expose them is gone.

tutorial.line: New tools. Phone records need a court order: a stamp, and a reason tying that number to this case.
A mast tells you the neighbourhood, not the door. Use it to narrow. Never to pin.
From now on Halima wants to know why. Who and why are judged separately. Get one right and she'll tell you.

ui.beatNotes: The records request (a form with the probable-cause fact pre-typed and a court-order stamp), the mast map (coverage circles over Old Town) and the WHY blank, confirmed as its own group. Mwalimu covers all three in under 30 seconds.
